passage: At the final-year project fair, four teams told how they had worked. Ganga's team of four cut the project into modules, pinned each job to a common board, with an owner and a date, and met briefly twice a week to review it. Aparna's group saw that the data pipeline had to exist before the model could be trained, while the interface could be built at the same time. So they gave the pipeline's owner extra help first. Ira's team was sure the project was easy. They put off coding till the last four weeks, then hit integration bugs and rushed out a barely working submission. Kunal's team missed a milestone twice. They asked why, again and again, and found that vague requirements, and not idleness, were the cause. They wrote a single-page specification and agreed what would count as done.

qa.q: How often did Ganga's team meet to review the board?
How does Ira's team's timing differ from Ganga's team's, and what did each end up with?
qa.a: Ira's team postponed coding to the final month and rushed a barely working project. Ganga's team spread jobs across modules with owners and dates, and reviewed them often.

qa.q: What might Ira's team be feeling as they scramble in the last month?
qa.a: They are probably stressed and regretful, because their confidence that the project was easy proved wrong.

qa.q: What could Ira's team try for the next big task?
qa.a: They could split the work into small pieces early, put dates on each and check progress every few days. Starting the hard parts first would show problems sooner. 🙂

grounding: Four final-year teams manage a project by splitting tasks, ordering dependencies, leaving it to the last month, and finding the root cause of a missed milestone.
